etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English writen, from Old English wrītan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrītan, from Proto-Germanic *wrītaną (“to carve, write”), from Proto-Indo-European *wrey- (“to rip, tear”).

Cognate with West Frisian write (“to wear by rubbing, rip, tear”), Dutch wrijten (“to argue, quarrel”), Middle Low German wrîten (“to scratch, draw, write”) (> Low German wrieten, rieten (“to tear, split”)), German reißen (“to tear, rip”), Norwegian rita (“to rough-sketch, carve, write”), Swedish rita (“to draw, design, delineate, model”), Icelandic rita (“to cut, scratch, write”), German ritzen (“to carve, scratch”), Proto-Slavic *ryti (“to carve, engrave, dig”), Polish ryć (“to engrave, dig”), Czech rýt (“to engrave, dig”). See also rit and rat.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To form letters, words or symbols on a surface in order to communicate.
(transitive) To be the author of (a book, article, poem, etc.).

quote.citation: 1892, Walter Besant, “Prologue: Who is Edmund Gray?”, in The Ivory Gate […], New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Thus, when he drew up instructions in lawyer language […]; his clerks, however, understood him very well. If he had written a love letter, or a farce, or a ballade, or a story, no one, either clerks, or friends, or compositors, would have understood anything but a word here and a word there.

quote.citation: 1964, Ernest Hemingway, A Moveable Feast, New York, N.Y.: Charles Scribner’s Sons, →OCLC, page 151:
quote.text: Since I had started to break down all my writing and get rid of all facility and try to make instead of describe, writing had been wonderful to do. But it was very difficult, and I did not know how I would ever write anything as long as a novel. It often took me a full morning of work to write a paragraph.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To show (information, etc) in written form.

quote.citation: 1957 September 30, “Ghana: White Eminence”, in Time‎[1], New York, N.Y.: Time Inc., →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 19 October 2011:
quote.text: Ghana's motto, writ large on the gleaming white Independence Arch that overlooks the Atlantic in Accra, is "Freedom and Justice."

quote.citation: 1959 August, K. Hoole, “The Middlesbrough–Newcastle Route of the N.E.R.”, in Trains Illustrated, London: Ian Allan Publishing, →ISSN, →OCLC, page 359:
quote.text: The route passes over low-lying land, the only item of note being the Cerebos salt works at Greatham, where one may catch a glimpse of the smart black diesel locomotive emblazoned with the firm's name writ large.

definitions.definition: (ditransitive with relative clause) To convey a fact to someone via writing.

quote.citation: 1916 March 11, “[advertisement] Jim Henry, Optimist”, in Saturday Evening Post‎[2]:
quote.text: Do you know, one man actually wrote me he thought he could almost shave with the back of the blade, the lather "mellowed" his beard so.

quote.citation: 1964, Ernest Hemingway, A Moveable Feast, page 151:
quote.text: I said that I did not believe anyone could write any way except the very best he could write without destroying his talent.

definitions.definition: (computing, intransitive, with to) To record data mechanically or electronically.
(transitive, South Africa, Canada, of an exam, a document, etc.) To fill in, to complete using words.

quote.citation: 2023, Ayọ̀bámi Adébáyọ̀, A Spell of Good Things, Canongate Books, page 132:
quote.text: Kúnlé had failed biology and chemistry, key requirements for admission into any medical school in the country. Kúnlé’s father wanted him to write the exams again.

definitions.definition: To impress durably; to imprint; to engrave.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Romans 2:14–15:
quote.text: 14 For when the Gentiles which haue not the Law, doe by nature the things contained in the Law: these hauing not the Law, are a Law vnto themselues,15 Which shew the worke of the Law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witnesse, and their thoughts the meane while accusing, or else excusing one another:

definitions.definition: To make known by writing; to record; to prove by one's own written testimony; often used reflexively.

quote.citation: c. 1587–1588, [Christopher Marlowe], Tamburlaine the Great.  […]  The First Part […], 2nd edition, part 1, London:  […]  [R. Robinson for] Richard Iones, […], published 1592, →OCLC; reprinted as Tamburlaine the Great (A Scolar Press Facsimile), Menston, Yorkshire, London: Scolar Press, 1973, →ISBN, Act III, scene iii:
quote.text: Thoſe walled garriſons will I ſubdue,And write my ſelfe great Lord of Affrica:So from the Eaſt vnto the furtheſt Weſt,Shall Tamburlaine extend his puiſant arme.

quote.citation: 1649, J[ohn] Milton, ΕΙΚΟΝΟΚΛΆΣΤΗΣ [Eikonoklástēs] […], London:  […]  Matthew Simmons, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: He who writes himself Martyr by his own inscription, is like an ill painter, who by writing on a shapeless picture which he hath drawn, is fain to tell passengers what shape it is, which else no man could imagine.

definitions.definition: (finance) To sell (an option or other derivative).
(chiefly Eastern Orthodoxy) To paint a religious icon.
The act or style of writing.

quote.text: The pen also gives a better write than the ordinary counter pen. The ink stand cannot be stolen, for it is fastened to the counter or desk.

definitions.definition: (computing) The operation of storing data, as in memory or onto disk.

quote.citation: 2006, MySQL administrator's guide and language reference, page 393:
quote.text: In other words, the system can do 1200 reads per second with no writes, the average write is twice as slow as the average read, and the relationship is linear.
